_note: Lore snippets a prompt may cite by id (request context.canon). The archive.* entries are the Archive's own in-world entries (data/lore/archive/*.md, imported from stapledons-design), flattened to one paragraph; the Archive's answers cite them (R1-ARCHIVE-VOICE). An unknown id makes the request a bad_request.

lore.archive.two-clocks: Every journey has two durations, and both are true. The galaxy keeps one clock. A trip to Alpha Centauri at 0.99c takes 4.414 years by that clock: the distance divided by your speed. Your own clock runs slower by the Lorentz factor, which at that speed is 7.0888. Aboard, the same trip takes 0.6227 years, about 227 days. You will step off younger than everyone you left will be when they hear you arrived. Going faster changes the balance. At 0.999999c the galaxy still counts 4.370 years, because nothing can beat light. Aboard, the trip lasts 2.26 days. Nothing about this is a trick of the instruments. Both clocks measure time, each in its own frame. The difference does not come back when you stop. The years at home have passed, and the days aboard are the only days you lived. For comparison, an old-fashioned rocket at a steady 1 g, turning around halfway, would reach a peak speed of 0.9517c. It would take 3.582 years aboard and 6.003 years at home. When you commit to a journey, the Archive shows both clocks and the years left at home. Read them slowly.
lore.archive.sol: Sol is the star the voyage left behind. The light the ship sees from it is always older than the last message home.
lore.archive.bubble: You live inside a sphere of radius 100 m, held by the generator in the spire. Inside it, the ordinary laws of physics hold as they always have. The bubble itself is what makes the voyage possible. It does three things. Its wall stops every particle that has mass, inward and outward, and lets light and neutrinos pass. Seen from outside, the whole pocket behaves as if it weighs very little, though never nothing. A pocket that weighed nothing would have to travel at exactly the speed of light, and your clocks would stop. And inside, the pocket keeps its own frame: when it accelerates, you do not feel it. It is called a Higgs bubble, but the name is a label, not an explanation. The Higgs field gives a proton only about 1% of its mass; the rest is the binding energy of the strong force. If the field were switched off inside, the electron would lose its mass and atoms would come apart. So inside the bubble, physics is normal. Everything else the Archive tells you about the voyage follows from those three properties: the drive, the glow, the sky, the danger near black holes. Ask about any of them.
lore.archive.weather-between-the-stars: The space around the Sun is patchy. We fly through clouds a few light years across, warm gas at about seven thousand kelvin with 0.2474 cm⁻³ hydrogen, and between them the hot gas of the Local Bubble, a million degrees and nearly empty at 3.9 × 10⁻³ cm⁻³. The Sun is just inside one cloud, the Local Interstellar Cloud. Alpha Centauri lies beyond another, the G cloud, and its light carries that cloud's hydrogen lines to us. The road to Aldebaran passes through the Hyades cloud. Astronomers mapped these clouds from the absorption lines they print on the light of nearby stars. The clouds carry dust. Most grains are smaller than the wavelength of light, but the Ulysses spacecraft, crossing the Sun's poles for sixteen years, caught grains far larger: up to 8.98 µm in radius, grains of solid rock. At our speeds every grain arrives with the energy of a bomb fragment. At ninety-nine point nine per cent of light speed, in a warm cloud, the wall meets 1,842 s⁻¹ grains of a micrometre or more. The wall turns them aside like the gas, and the fraction that is not elastic flashes on the forward dome. In the warm clouds the flashes glitter under the glow; in the hot bubble they are fewer, and each one stands out. Clouds also set a limit. Holding a cruise speed means pushing against the drag everywhere along it. In the warm clouds our drive can hold any speed up to a Lorentz factor of 2,117. Denser gas lowers that limit. A route the drive cannot hold is refused, and the captain chooses: slow down, or go around by way of another star. (The cloud outlines on the chart come from the published sky surveys. How far each cloud reaches along the line of sight is the Archive's best estimate, and it is refined as the ship crosses them.)
lore.archive.nothing-crosses: The wall is absolute for anything with mass. No dust, no gas, no gift from a stranger, no crew member stepping outside. What you brought is what you have. Light crosses freely, in both directions, at every colour and energy. That is the one part of the wall that real physics already allows, because light does not feel the Higgs field. Neutrinos cross too. They pass through planets as easily as through the hull, and the wall lets them be. There was once a belief aboard that a trickle of hydrogen leaked in from space. It does not, and it must not. Near the speed of light, the thin gas between the stars arrives as a beam. At 0.999999c every proton would strike with an energy of 663.5 GeV, more than many particle accelerators reach. A leaking wall would be a weapon pointed at the bow. So the ledger is closed. Births, meals, repairs and new machines are all made from mass already aboard. Nothing material leaves either, only light: the light the drive emits, and the faint light of the boundary glow. You carry ideas, not cargo. Everything you learn from the galaxy arrives as light.
lore.archive.earths-voice: Earth is always behind you in time. The newest light from home that reaches the ship left Earth as many years ago as you are light-years away. At every port, the news is exactly as old as the distance. Moving changes how fast that old news arrives. Flying straight away from home at 0.99c, each hour aboard brings you 0.070888 of an hour of Earth's history. At 0.999999c it is 7.0711 × 10⁻⁴, and home slows almost to stillness. Turn for home at that speed and the same history pours in 1414.2 times faster than you live it. A message sent after you leave has to chase you. Sent one day behind a ship at 0.9c, it catches up 10 days after departure. Behind a ship at 0.999999c it needs 2,737.9 years. Earth beams only toward plans it has heard. Change course far from home and your new plan takes years to reach Earth, and Earth's answer takes years more to reach your new port. Turn at right angles from a port forty light-years out, thirty light-years across, and the light's path through home is 60 ly longer than your own. You wait that many years at the new port before Earth's voice finds you again. Until then, Earth keeps speaking toward the place you left.
lore.archive.following-light: To keep its voice on you, Earth must aim at a ship crossing its sky at nearly the speed of light. It sounds impossible. Distance makes it gentle. A ship crossing Earth's sky at 0.99c, forty light-years out, moves Earth's aim by only 1.418° a year. The Moon moves farther than that across your old sky in an evening. Earth has to turn fastest when you fly away from it almost along its line of sight, just to one side. Then its light chases you along your path, and the aim swings faster by your Lorentz factor. At 0.999999c, forty light-years out, that is 2.773° a day. One light-year from home it is 110.9° a day. Even that is slower than Earth's own turning, which every telescope on it already follows. The hard part is not turning but knowing where to turn. The light Earth sees from you left years ago, from a place you have long since passed. So Earth never aims at what it sees. It aims where your committed course says you will be when its light arrives, the way a hunter leads a bird. Earth's first laser links to deep space already aimed ahead of their spacecraft [cite: NASA Deep Space Optical Communications aboard Psyche, 2023]. This is why your plan must reach home before Earth can follow you. Without it, Earth would be aiming at a memory.
